$comment: The site's pack map, declared. A map that says zero is a decision, and a page
with no map is a drift; this is the file the check and the test both read, so
there is one expectation and two independent readers of it: this repository's
DOM (a test that renders the real composition) and this repository's built
export (the script below, which reads the emitted HTML and the emitted CSS).
The rule being enforced, in one sentence: a pack boundary lands on a mark and
nowhere else, and exactly one region of a page may carry a pack that is not the
page's own ground.
**There were two regions and there is one, and the one that left is the one the
bar changed.** The header used to carry a row of five product marks at first
paint, which is what `header.switcher` declared. The bar is now the design
system's `SiteNavbar` and the family set is a menu, so those marks are rendered
when a reader opens the menu rather than when the page loads, and a static export
emits no menu that has not been opened. This gate reads the emitted HTML, so it
reads a page with no switcher in it, and a region declared for marks the page does
not carry is a finding in both readers rather than a stale entry nobody notices.
That is a real change to the page and not only to this file. The first paint now
carries one pack boundary fewer, and four non-ground pastels moved from above the
fold into a control. What is left is the products band on the landing, which is
the better half to keep on the page for the reason the law gives: a boundary may
only land on a ProductMark, so a mark is the one element that can wear a hue other
than the ground's, and the reader deciding which product a row is talking about
is a decision made from that mark.
The second half of the rule is arithmetic rather than taste. A boundary
re-points --radius, and this page's ground is lavender at 0.75rem while the other
four packs run 0.5rem to 1rem, so a section wearing a second pack would put that
section's index into its corner radius. And a section ground puts the pack's hue
into every status dot and every primary-filled control inside it, which is what
the old rule protected against when it forbade pack grounds for a reason that no
longer exists. That old rule is gone; this is what is left of it, and it is
checkable.
`regions` lists every region that carries a boundary at all, with the exact
multiset of packs each one carries, so a boundary added by accident is a finding
in both readers. `secondPackRegions` is the rule restated, and it is asserted as
well as derived: a page that grows a second region carrying a second pack fails
the build.
The region names come from the structure the catalogue publishes, which is the
same rule `scripts/pack-regions.mjs` states. One of them used to be named after
the ordinal its own band printed above its heading, so the map depended on a
number the page put there for a reader and the gate read for a machine. The page
no longer prints an ordinal, and the region is named `landing.products` after the
Block that draws the rows.

header.brand.why: The bar's brand lockup is this site, and this site's pack is the page's pack, so its boundary is the ground rather than a second pack.

footer.brand.why: The same lockup, in the footer. A ground is stable for the life of a page, and a footer that wore a different hue from the page it closes would be a second claim about the same thing.

landing.products.why: A product row's mark is that product's own hue, and it is the one claim on this page a reader makes a decision from: which product is this, and does its colour mean anything. The mark is a fully rounded disc, so the boundary moves nothing about its shape. The region is named by the Block that draws the rows rather than by the ordinal the band used to print, so a page that renumbers its sections does not silently rename a region the gate holds it to. This band is the second of the two the page used to have: the old page drew the same three products as cards with a hand-written dot that carried no background at all, so the reader saw three names and no marks.
